Joyce Echaquan est décédée à l’hôpital d: Joyce Echaquan died at the Joliette hospital last Monday, shortly after filming herself on Facebook to ask for help as nurses hurled racist insults at her. “Joyce could only denounce the situation with her phone, and that’s why we know what happened to her, but it happens every day and we don’t always have the means to film it,” said Nakuset, executive director of the Native Women’s Shelter of Montreal, last Wednesday.
La mort de la femme atikamekw pousse plu: The death of the Atikamekw woman has led many Indigenous people to publicly denounce, on social media and in the press, the racism they experience or have experienced in the health care system.

C’est en apprenant l’histoire de Joyce q: It was when she learned Joyce’s story that Christina Bégin felt she needed to speak about her own experience at the Joliette hospital nearly 30 years ago. In 1992, Christina was pregnant with her son. She went to the Joliette hospital to give birth by C-section. During the operation, she woke up and heard the gynecologist make several racist comments about Indigenous people. “He said Indigenous people were all a bunch of alcoholics,” <l1>she told us at the vigil held for Joyce Echaquan in front of the Joliette hospital. </l1>Christina then moved her head to show that she was conscious.
« L’infirmier s’est rendu compte que j’é: “The nurse realized I was awake and told the gynecologist, but he said, ‘It’s no big deal, she’ll go back to sleep.’ I know he said other degrading things about me, but I don’t remember them, because I fell back asleep right after.”
Le lendemain, elle se réveille en pleurs: The next day, she woke up in tears and told the nurse, who did not follow up on the incident. “She didn’t even come to comfort me,” she said sadly. Her cousin also once confided that she had had a similar problem with the same doctor. “It’s been eating at me since yesterday, I’d like to file a complaint. I hope it’s not too late.”

Georges-Hervé Awashish à l’hôpital de Ch: Georges-Hervé Awashish at the Chicoutimi hospital. Photo: Courtesy of Shawnok Awashish
Si le drame survenu à Joliette donne le: While the tragedy in Joliette gave Christina Dubé the courage to speak out about the past, others are denouncing what they are living right now, like Georges-Hervé Awashish. He was admitted to the Chicoutimi hospital last week. He has several health problems that require specialized care. So it is from his hospital room that he gave us a telephone interview. He wants to share his experience “so people know what’s going on with Indigenous people,” he tells us quietly over the phone.
Deux jours après la mort de Joyce Echaqu: Two days after the death of Joyce Echaquan, the Atikamekw man from Obedjiwan says he heard nursing staff at the Chicoutimi hospital make death threats against him. In the night from Wednesday to Thursday, around 3 a.m., he got up to go to the bathroom. When he came back to his room on the fourth floor, he heard staff talking in the hallway.
« Ils parlaient de Manawan, de M. Echaqu: “They were talking about Manawan, about Mr. Echaquan, and they were laughing,” he says. Shaken, Mr. Awashish did not say a word in his room, which is close to the nurses’ station. He sat down in his wheelchair. “After that, I heard one of the nurses say, ‘We got one, we got an Indian here, lying in the room.’ And then another one said, ‘We should inject him with something toxic, and his problem will be solved, he’ll suffer anyway.’ After that, they started laughing. They were laughing in the hallway,” he recounts. Frozen, Georges-Hervé Awashish said nothing.
Après avoir retrouvé son sang-froid, il: After regaining his composure, he phoned his son and paid for a taxi so he could come get him. “He called me in the night so I’d come get him, he didn’t want to tell me over the phone what had happened,” says Shawnok Awashish. “He was traumatized. After hearing the death threats, he couldn’t lie down in his room anymore,” he continues.
Quelques heures plus tard, M. Awashish a: A few hours later, Mr. Awashish left the hospital with his son. A nurse who reportedly heard her colleagues’ remarks tried to keep them from leaving, say Georges-Hervé and Shawnok. After the incident, Georges-Hervé stayed at his sister Louisette’s home in La Baie, next to Chicoutimi. He did not want to go back to the hospital. But his health problems require him to get medical follow-up.
« La police est venue me chercher chez m: “The police came to get me at my sister’s place to take me to the hospital on Saturday,” he says. He is now on the second floor of the hospital, where his doctor reportedly assured him that no one from the fourth floor will come harass him. But Mr. Awashish is far from reassured: he fears for his life. “I can’t sleep, I’m not comfortable here, I hear their voices in my head. I have to take pills for anxiety,” confides the 53-year-old, who says he is afraid of suffering the same fate as Joyce Echaquan. “My life is at stake, I’m very anxious. What’s happening is really disappointing, I find it really disappointing.”
Dans un courriel envoyé à La Converse, l: In an email sent to La Converse, the Centre intégré universitaire de santé et de services sociaux du Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean confirmed that an investigation was opened last Thursday following the alleged events.
« Nous en sommes à colliger l’informatio: “We are currently gathering information and validating the facts. If such a situation were to prove true, it is clear to our institution that it is a shocking and unacceptable event,” said Amélie Gourde of communications and government affairs. Asked whether the staff members denounced by Mr. Awashish are still on the job, the CIUSSS du Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean said no measures would be taken before the investigation report is submitted and that, at this stage, these are still allegations. The team of Mr. Awashish’s doctor, Mathieu Leblanc, directed us to the institution’s media relations, which refused to let us interview him. For his part, Georges-Hervé says he is waiting to leave the hospital where he received death threats.
